title: Finding a Qualified OT, SLP, or PT
body:
Occupational therapists (OT), speech-language pathologists (SLP), and physical therapists (PT) all require licensure, but the specifics of what to check differ slightly by discipline — and pediatric, autism-specific experience is worth screening for separately from the license itself.

Start with credentials. In the U.S., look for state licensure plus, ideally, national certification: OTs often hold an OTR credential (Occupational Therapist, Registered), SLPs typically hold the ASHA Certificate of Clinical Competence (CCC-SLP), and PTs are licensed DPTs. Ask directly whether the therapist is licensed in your state and in good standing — most state licensing boards have a public lookup tool.

Ask about pediatric and autism-specific experience, not just general experience. A therapist can be fully licensed and excellent with adults but have limited experience with autistic children specifically. Ask how many autistic clients they currently see, what approaches they use, and whether they tailor sessions to a child's specific sensory or communication needs.

Ask how progress is measured. A good therapist should be able to describe concrete, observable goals for your child and how they'll track progress toward them — not just "we'll see how it goes."

Finally, trust your own observations. Even a well-credentialed therapist may not be the right fit if your child seems consistently distressed by sessions or you don't see any adjustment to their approach over time. It's reasonable to seek a second opinion or switch providers if something feels off.
